explanations.answer: Rejoice and let your heart be glad
explanations.explanation: That's it, friend. The Teacher, a king in Jerusalem (Ecclesiastes 1:1), says, "Rejoice, O young man, while you are young, and let your heart be glad in the days of your youth." Notice he opens with gladness. I've heard plenty of advice in my day, and a king telling you to be glad is the kind I'd frame on the bakery wall.

explanations.answer: Labor and let your hands be busy
explanations.explanation: Close, but that's not what the Teacher says here. He is a king in Jerusalem (Ecclesiastes 1:1), and his words to the young man are "Rejoice, O young man, while you are young, and let your heart be glad in the days of your youth." Busy hands are a fine thing, and my mustache has the cramps to prove it. But this verse is about a glad heart.

explanations.answer: Be still and let your face be sober
explanations.explanation: Not this time. The Teacher, a king in Jerusalem (Ecclesiastes 1:1), says, "Rejoice, O young man, while you are young, and let your heart be glad in the days of your youth." A sober face is not in the order. It's a glad heart, friend, and I think a smile follows right behind it.

True. The Teacher says, "Walk in the ways of your heart and in the sight of your eyes, but know that for all these things God will bring you to judgment." Right after all that gladness comes a quiet "but know." He lets the young man enjoy the road and still tells him plainly that God will bring him to judgment.

It's actually true, friend. Here's what the verse says: "Walk in the ways of your heart and in the sight of your eyes, but know that for all these things God will bring you to judgment." The Teacher says it right in the middle of his words about being young. It's easy to skip past a "but" when the part before it sounds so good.

Fleeting is right. The Teacher says, "So banish sorrow from your heart, and cast off pain from your body, for youth and vigor are fleeting." Vigor means strength, and he's saying it doesn't stay. It's like a fresh cookie on the cooling rack at my place. It looks like it will be there forever, and then I turn around.

The verse says the opposite. The Teacher says, "…for youth and vigor are fleeting." Endless would make the rest of his words sound strange, because he's telling the young man to banish sorrow while there's time. Fleeting means it passes, friend.
Good guess, but the Teacher never calls youth wasted. He says, "…for youth and vigor are fleeting." He isn't scolding anybody here. I think he's saying youth is real and good, and it doesn't last.

That's the one. The Teacher says, "Remember your Creator in the days of your youth, before the days of adversity come…" He puts the remembering first and the hard days after. A smart baker preheats the oven before the dough is ready, and this is the same idea.
Not quite. The text says, "Remember your Creator in the days of your youth, before the days of adversity come…" Plenty isn't mentioned. The Teacher is looking ahead to adversity, friend.

Harvest sounds like a good guess, but it's not in this verse. The Teacher says to remember your Creator "…before the days of adversity come…" Those are the days he has in mind. He doesn't mention a harvest at all.

explanations.answer: I find no pleasure in them
explanations.explanation: Yes. The Teacher says "…the years approach of which you will say, “I find no pleasure in them,”" (Ecclesiastes 12:1). That's what a person says about those years. It's a heavy line, so I'll just say it plainly: I think it's meant to make us listen.

explanations.answer: I wish they would never end
explanations.explanation: That's the opposite of what the text says. The Teacher says "…the years approach of which you will say, “I find no pleasure in them,”" (Ecclesiastes 12:1). Nobody in this verse is begging for those years to last. They are years the person says have no pleasure in them.

Not in this verse. The text says "…the years approach of which you will say, “I find no pleasure in them,”" (Ecclesiastes 12:1). The Teacher had already said that youth and vigor are fleeting (Ecclesiastes 11:10). These are different years.

It's actually false. The Teacher says the light is darkened "…and the clouds return after the rain…" Returning clouds are the opposite of a clear sky. Anybody who has hung out laundry knows that feeling, and I'm sorry you had to learn it here.
False is right. The verse says, "…before the light of the sun, moon, and stars is darkened, and the clouds return after the rain…" The clouds come back. That's a gray picture, friend.

It's the other way around. The text says, "…on the day the keepers of the house tremble and the strong men stoop…" Stoop means bending over, and that's not standing tall. Even the strong ones in this house are bowing low, friend.
False, and you read that right. The verse says the keepers of the house tremble "…and the strong men stoop…" The strong men are bent over. Even the strong ones in this picture are bowing low, friend.

That's right. The verse says, "…when those grinding cease because they are few…" The work stops because those grinding are few. It's like a bakery shift where everybody went home and left me alone with the mixer. Wait, I'm alone with the mixer every day.
The text doesn't say that. It says, "…when those grinding cease because they are few…" The reason is that the grinders are few. Nothing is said about the grain running out.

Nobody sells the mill in this verse. The text says, "…when those grinding cease because they are few…" The grinders are few, friend, and that's the whole reason. The next verse says the sound of the mill fades away, but it never says why a mill would be sold.
Yes, the bird. The verse says "…when one rises at the sound of a bird…" In the Teacher's picture, that's the sound a person rises at. Just a bird, friend, and up the person goes.
No bell in this verse. The text says "…when one rises at the sound of a bird…" A person rises at the sound of a bird, not a bell. Bells are lovely, but they aren't in this line.
Nice try, but no watchman is calling out here. The verse says "…when one rises at the sound of a bird…" Just a bird, friend. That's the sound named in this line.

It's actually false. The text says, "…when men fear the heights and dangers of the road…" They fear them, which is the opposite of bold. That's a long way from the young man who was told to walk in the ways of his heart (Ecclesiastes 11:9).

False is right. The verse says, "…when men fear the heights and dangers of the road…" Nobody is bolder here, friend. They fear the heights and the dangers of the road. I think we all know a ladder that looks taller than it did last year.
That's it. The verse says "…for then man goes to his eternal home and mourners walk the streets." The Teacher says it quietly and plainly. It's a heavy line, friend.
No Egypt here. The text says "…for then man goes to his eternal home…" Egypt isn't mentioned anywhere in this verse, friend. Mourners are walking the streets in it, so it's a serious one.

Not a far country, though I see why you'd guess it. The verse says "…for then man goes to his eternal home and mourners walk the streets." The Teacher calls it his eternal home. This is a heavy part, and I think it's meant to be.

Right on. The silver cord is "snapped," the golden bowl is "crushed," the pitcher is "shattered" and the wheel is "broken" (Ecclesiastes 12:6). Four different things, and each one is broken. That's the thread running through the whole verse.

explanations.answer: Each one is made of gold
explanations.explanation: Not every one. The cord is silver and the bowl is golden, but the verse doesn't say what the pitcher or the wheel are made of. What they all share is that each one is broken: snapped, crushed, shattered and broken (Ecclesiastes 12:6).

That's not what the verse says, friend. It says the silver cord is "snapped," the golden bowl is "crushed," the pitcher is "shattered" and the wheel is "broken" (Ecclesiastes 12:6). Being broken is what the four share. The verse says nothing about any of them being new.
Ground is right. The verse says "…before the dust returns to the ground from which it came…" The dust goes back to where it came from. This is a quiet, heavy line, and I'll leave it that way.
Yes, God. The verse says "…and the spirit returns to God who gave it." The one who gave the spirit is the one it returns to. It's the last gentle word in the Teacher's picture.
The sea isn't in this verse. The text says "…before the dust returns to the ground from which it came…" Dust goes back to the ground, friend. It's a quiet verse, and the ground is where it lands.

Stars light up my sky, but they don't show up in this verse. The text says "…before the dust returns to the ground from which it came and the spirit returns to God who gave it." The dust returns to the ground, and the spirit returns to God. Those are the two answers, and the stars stay put.
No river here, friend. The verse says "…before the dust returns to the ground from which it came…" The ground is the answer for dust. The spirit goes to God, who gave it.

True. The last line of the passage says, "'Futility of futilities,' says the Teacher. 'Everything is futile!'" It's a hard thing to end on, and it comes right after the Teacher's pictures of the dust and the spirit (Ecclesiastes 12:7). I think it's worth sitting with for a second.

The Teacher actually does say it. The passage ends with "'Futility of futilities,' says the Teacher. 'Everything is futile!'" That's his last word here, friend. It's a heavy line, and I won't pretend it isn't.
